lesson.menu_title: Five Minutes, One Message -- Presentation Skills
lesson.menu_desc: Structure a short update so the room can follow it: discourse markers that tell the listener what is coming, plus the words of a short talk -- outline, hook, signpost, headline, rehearse, pace, filler, attention span, call to action, handout
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 28 -- Five Minutes, One Message
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 28 -- Five Minutes, One Message
lesson.grammar_point: discourse markers for structuring a talk (to begin with / having said that / as a result / that brings me to)

paras: Most updates to a board fail in the first thirty seconds, and not because the news is bad. They fail because the audience does not know where the speaker is going. To begin with, then, a good five-minute update needs a hook: one sentence that tells the room why these five minutes matter to them, not to you.

Having said that, a hook is not a joke, and it is not a story about your weekend. It is the headline of the whole talk. "The June shipment will be two weeks late unless we decide today" is a hook. "I want to share some logistics updates" is not. As a result of that one sentence, everyone at the table starts listening for the decision.

Turning to the middle, the rule is three points and no more. Each point gets its own signpost -- "first", "the second issue", "that brings me to" -- so that a listener who drifted for ten seconds can find the way back. In other words, signposts are not decoration; they are for the people whose attention span is shorter than your talk. Fillers such as "basically" and "so, yeah" do the opposite: they tell the room nothing and cost you authority.

Finally, end with a call to action, not a summary of what you have already said. If you need approval, ask for it by name. Rehearse the opening and the ending aloud at least twice, at a slower pace than feels natural, and put the numbers in a one-page handout rather than on a crowded slide. Five minutes is enough time for one decision. It is never enough time for everything you know.

listenings.text: Thank you all for making the time. I have five minutes, and I am going to use them for one message: our Houston warehouse will be full by October unless we act this quarter. To begin with, the numbers. Volume through the warehouse is up eighteen percent since January, and we are already renting overflow space by the week, which is the most expensive way to store anything. Having said that, this is a good problem. It exists because sales are ahead of plan, not behind it. That brings me to the options. There are two. The first is to extend our lease on the building next door, which can be done within six weeks. The second is to move slow-moving stock to a partner in Dallas, which is cheaper, but it adds two days to every delivery in that category. In other words, we can pay in money or we can pay in time. Because of the lease terms, the first option has to be approved by the end of this month. So here is what I am asking for today: a decision between the two, and if it is the lease, approval to sign it by the thirtieth. The details are in the handout, and I am happy to take questions.

The best presentation I ever gave had one slide, and it was the one I almost did not use. I was presenting a restructuring plan to a family board, and I had prepared twenty-two slides, because I wanted them to see how much work was behind it. The night before, I rehearsed it out loud for the first time, and it took nineteen minutes. I had seven. So I did something painful. I wrote down the single sentence I needed them to remember, and I asked myself whether each slide helped that sentence, or only helped me look prepared. Twenty-one slides went into a handout. The one that stayed had three numbers on it and nothing else. On the day, I opened with the sentence, I gave them the three numbers, and I asked for the decision. It took five minutes. Having said that, the most important moment was not in the talk at all. It was the silence after I asked for the decision, which I did not fill. In other words, the pause did the work. They approved the plan that afternoon.

extra_audio.text: First, you write one sentence that the audience must remember, and you build the whole outline around it. Then, you open with a hook that tells the room why these five minutes matter to them, and not to you. After that, you give the first point, starting with a marker such as to begin with, so that the room knows the talk has begun. Next, you signpost the move to each new point, so that anyone who drifted for a moment can find the way back. Finally, you end with a call to action, you ask for the decision by name, and then you stop talking.
